blocks.content: The orange cat in the antique shop window has never acknowledged me.

Not once. Not a flick of the ear. Not a slow blink. I've been running past that window for two years and the cat looks through me with the specific contempt of something that knows exactly how the power dynamic works. I've started finding it motivating. If that cat can be that completely unbothered by my existence, I can survive the second mile.

The bookstore is still dark at this hour. Whoever owns it opens late and closes early, and I have never once seen them change the window display, which currently has three novels arranged around a ceramic owl that has definitely been there since before I moved to this neighborhood. I find it comforting. Some things stay.

Mrs. Okafor was out with her dog at the corner of Bellamy, same as always. The dog — whose name I have never learned but whom I think of privately as Gerald — lifted his head as I passed. Mrs. Okafor did not look up from her phone. Gerald and I have an understanding.

I'm freelance. Nineteen years old, running through a town I mostly like, trying to make enough from painting to justify the decision to paint full-time instead of the thing my mom keeps bringing up. I do not say the word. I just run.

Last week I finished a commission for a guy who wanted his motorcycle floating in outer space. Pale blue background, stars pulled from a reference photo of the actual Milky Way, the bike dead center with the chrome catching fake starlight. He cried when he saw it. I charged him two hundred dollars, which was too little, but he seemed like he needed the cry more than I needed the difference.
That's mostly what freelancing is. Noticing what people need and finding the version of it you can give them.
The Copper Mug glowed at the end of the block.
